mcqs.question: Two objects reference only each other, and the one outside reference to either of them has just been dropped. Under a tracing collector, what determines whether they're garbage?
options: Whether their combined reference count is above zero
Whether either object is still reachable by following pointers from the root set
Whether they were allocated in the same collection cycle
Whether the objects have a finalizer defined
mcqs.explanation: Tracing GC's test is reachability from roots, not a count — since neither object is reachable from any root anymore, both are correctly identified as garbage in one pass with no special cycle handling. Reference count, allocation timing, and finalizers play no role in this determination.

mcqs.question: In the mark pseudocode, why does checking `obj.marked` before recursing matter beyond just avoiding duplicate work?
options: It's what makes the traversal correctly terminate on cyclic object graphs instead of recursing forever
It reduces the memory footprint of the marked objects themselves
It's required so the sweep phase can run in a separate thread
It converts the recursive traversal into a sorting operation
mcqs.explanation: Without the visited check, a cycle in the object graph would send mark() into infinite recursion, re-entering the same objects forever — the check is what makes cycles safe, not just efficient. It has no bearing on memory footprint, threading, or sorting.

mcqs.question: Why does a naive tracing collector need to stop every application thread during the mark phase?
options: To reduce the total number of objects that need to be marked
Because marking requires exclusive access to the CPU cache
To let the sweep phase run concurrently with mark
Because mutating a pointer mid-trace could cause the collector to miss an object that's actually still live and free it incorrectly
mcqs.explanation: The trace needs a consistent snapshot of the pointer graph — if the mutator changes a reference the collector hasn't visited yet while the collector is mid-trace elsewhere, correctness breaks and a live object can get freed. Stopping the world is the simple fix; it doesn't reduce the object count, and CPU cache access isn't the underlying reason.

mcqs.question: Mark-compact eliminates fragmentation that mark-sweep leaves behind. What does it cost to do that?
options: It has to find and update every pointer to a moved object's new address, on top of the mark phase's cost
Nothing extra — compaction runs during idle CPU time for free
It requires the heap to be pre-allocated at twice its normal size
It skips the mark phase entirely and compacts based on allocation order
mcqs.explanation: Sliding survivors together only closes the gaps if every reference to a moved object is rewritten to its new address, which means the collector must find and update those pointers — real, additional work beyond sweep's simple free-list append. It still needs the mark phase, doesn't require idle time or double heap size to function.

mcqs.question: A heap is 90% dead objects at collection time. Which phase's cost stays roughly the same regardless of that ratio?
options: The mark phase, since it only visits the 10% that's live
Both phases shrink proportionally with the dead-object ratio
The sweep phase, since it walks every slot in the whole heap to check marks
Neither phase's cost depends on the heap in any way
mcqs.explanation: Sweep has to examine every slot in the full heap to know whether each one was marked, so its cost tracks total heap size regardless of how much is garbage. Mark, by contrast, only visits the live 10% and gets cheaper as the dead ratio grows — the opposite of what the sweep phase does.

mcqs.question: A service using a garbage-collected language slowly runs out of memory over days, and a heap dump shows a static map that only ever grows. Why doesn't the GC reclaim it?
options: The GC has a bug that fails to trace static fields
Static collections are excluded from garbage collection by design in every language
The objects in the map must have finalizers blocking their collection
The map is reachable from a root (the static field), so it is legitimately live from the collector's point of view — this is a logical leak, not a collector failure
mcqs.explanation: A static field is part of the root set, so anything reachable through it is correctly marked live — the collector is working exactly as designed, even though the data will never actually be used again. This is a logical leak the programmer created, not a bug in the GC, a language-wide exclusion, or a finalizer issue.
